turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Yeah, I know what "handle" means. It means your director has already decided something and is waiting to see if you'll do the uncomfortable thing yourself or need to be pushed.

But before you accept that framing — can I ask what you actually know? Not what the release timeline says, but what's actually happening in Suresh-ji's module. Is he not delivering because he's checked out? Because the work has moved somewhere he never got trained? Because he's carrying twelve years of legacy code nobody else understands and every change takes him three weeks of archaeology? Those are four completely different problems and only one of them is a performance problem.

Nineteen years and everyone calls him Suresh-ji — that's not just seniority, that's someone who's held things together for a long time. Which cuts both ways. It might mean he's the reason a lot of things still work. It might also mean nobody has given him honest feedback in a decade because it felt disrespectful, and he genuinely doesn't know he's the bottleneck.

That second possibility is the one that should scare you a little. Because if it's true, the first honest conversation is going to land like a slap, and it won't be his fault that it does.

What's your read? You've been in the seat four months — have you actually sat with him one-on-one and asked what's hard, or have you been reading it off dashboards and standups?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Okay, so this isn't a performance problem you're stuck on. It's the fact that you owe him something and the org is asking you to spend it.

And I want to name that honestly: you do owe him something. He covered for you when you were 24 and terrified. That was real. It's not a debt he's calling in, which somehow makes it heavier.

But here's the thing — the way you repay it isn't by protecting him from the truth. It's by being the one person who tells him honestly, in private, before it becomes a document with his name on it. What he did for you was give you a chance to recover without a permanent mark. That's what you can give him. Not silence — silence is what lets this end with an HR letter in eight months.

Please don't bring the slide. Not the first time. A deck turns him into a case, and it will humiliate him in a way he won't come back from. Go sit with him, close the door, and say something true and plain — "Suresh-ji, I need to talk to you about something difficult, and I'm telling you first because I don't want you to hear it from anyone else." Then tell him what you're seeing on the module, and ask him what's really going on. Then shut up and listen, even if it's uncomfortably long.

You may find out something you didn't expect. Nineteen years in, at 56, watching the stack move away from everything you were expert in — that's a specific kind of quiet terror, and men of his generation often don't have any language for asking for help with it.

Ask him what he wants the next four years to look like. There might be a real answer there that isn't "managed out" — legacy ownership, mentoring, the systems knowledge nobody's documented. Or there might not be. But you'll know, and you'll have asked.

One more thing — the "like my daughter" line. He meant it kindly. But you can't manage from inside that role. You'll have to gently step out of it in that conversation, and that's going to cost you something too. Are you ready for him to look at you differently afterward?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I'm not going to give you a clean yes, because you'd know I was just soothing you and it wouldn't hold past Sunday night.

Here's my honest answer: about 70% yes. The books are right that withholding feedback is the real disrespect. Where they're wrong for *this* conversation is the order of operations. Radical candor was written for people who talk to their reports constantly and have earned the right to be blunt. You've been his manager four months and nobody's told him anything hard in a decade. Leading with metrics on Monday isn't candor, it's an ambush with footnotes.

Flip it. Open with the concern in one plain sentence — "the module has slipped two releases and I'm worried" — then ask him what's happening, and actually listen. The data comes *second*, as confirmation, not as prosecution. Same directness. Same information. Completely different thing happening in the room.

And don't book a conference room. Everyone will see it on his calendar and know. Walk over, ask him for twenty minutes somewhere quiet.

The other thing I'd say — go in without knowing the ending. You're preparing like there's a script where you deliver Message A and he receives it. Real version: he might get defensive, or go very quiet, or tell you something that reframes the whole thing. Your job Monday isn't to land the message perfectly. It's to open the conversation honestly and stay in it.

You're not spiralling because you don't know what to do. You're spiralling because you do know, and it's going to hurt. The books can't fix that part. Nothing can.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

There may not be a version where you don't feel like the villain. That's the part I think you're actually asking me to fix, and I can't. But feeling like the villain and being one aren't the same thing, and you're going to have to learn to hold that gap, because management is basically living in it.

Look at what you're really comparing. Option one: you tell him the truth, give him a real shot, support it properly — and it still ends in a PIP. Then he leaves knowing someone fought for him and told him straight. Option two: you get the module moved, he coasts four years in a quiet corner while people route around him, and he slowly figures out he's been made irrelevant without anyone respecting him enough to say why. And "coasting to retirement" isn't as safe as it sounds — the next reorg, the next director, someone with no chai and no Diwali history looks at the org chart and cuts him with a form letter. You won't be there to soften it.

The mercy option isn't mercy. It's just you being spared the conversation.

And notice — you keep saying "the girl he treated like a daughter." That's the frame that's killing you. Someone who loves you can also need to tell you something hard. Fathers get told hard things by their daughters. It's not betrayal. It's what happens when the relationship survives into adulthood.

One practical thing: if it does come to a PIP, don't let it be the first he's hearing of it, and don't let it be paperwork-only. Fight for the training budget, the reassignment, the legacy-owner role — actually fight, on record. Then whatever happens, you'll know you spent your capital on him, not on your own comfort.

Have you got anyone you can talk to about this on Sunday night? Not for advice. Just so you're not sitting with it alone.
